title: 3Sum Closest
description: Find the triple whose sum is closest to a target by combining a fixed element with converging pointers.

data.text: Given an integer array `nums` and a `target`, return the sum of three elements that is **closest** to `target`. Exactly one answer is guaranteed to be closest.
Test every combination of three elements. O(n³), which is unusable beyond a few hundred elements.

data.title: Brute Force O(n³)

data.text: Sort the array. Fix the first element `i`, then use converging pointers on the remaining section to find the pair closest to `target - nums[i]`. Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan costs O(n²).

data.title: Sort + Two Pointers O(n²)
data.content: Fix one index, converge the other two.

data.title: Early exit when the sum equals the target
data.text: Distance zero is unbeatable, so returning immediately on `sum == target` is a legitimate optimisation and also removes any ambiguity about tie-breaking.

data.title: Difference from 3Sum
data.text: 3Sum asks for an exact zero sum and must skip duplicate triples. Here you are minimising distance, so duplicates do not matter and the duplicate-skipping logic can be removed entirely. This is a common follow-up question.

data.caption: After sorting, one index is fixed while the other two converge toward the target sum.
data.definition:
graph TD
    A["sorted [-4,-1,1,2] target=1"] --> B["i=0 (-4): left=-1 right=2 sum=-3, need larger"]
    B --> C["left=1 right=2 sum=-1, need larger"]
    C --> D["i=1 (-1): left=1 right=2 sum=2, dist=1, best=2"]
    D --> E["i=2: not enough elements, stop"]
    E --> F["return 2"]
    style F fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The 'fix one index, two-pointer the rest' shape reduces any k-sum problem by one dimension: 3Sum becomes O(n²), and 4Sum with the same idea becomes O(n³). Sorting first is what makes the converging pointers valid.
